cards.q: Many software developers write numbers in hexadecimal instead of binary. Which is an advantage of hexadecimal?
cards.right: Shorter: each hex digit stands for 4 bits
wrong: It takes up less memory in the computer
Each hex digit stands for a whole byte
The CPU processes hex faster than binary
cards.why: Hex is concise: one hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so the byte 11001001 is just C9. Fewer digits means fewer mistakes, and converting to binary is quick.
cards.hook: 16 = 2⁴: one hex digit is one nibble of 4 bits.
keys: one hex digit is exactly 4 bits

cards.q: Hexadecimal is used because it is easy for humans to read and write. Which of these is it a convenient way to show?
cards.right: Memory addresses and colour codes
cards.why: Hex is a compact way to show binary values to people: memory addresses, machine code, error codes and colours like #0A33F0. It doesn't encrypt or compress anything.
cards.hook: Hex is just binary written short, for humans.
keys: compact way to show binary values to people

cards.q: Convert the hexadecimal number C9 into a decimal number.
cards.hook: Left hex digit counts 16s. A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15.

cards.q: The hexadecimal number C9 can be converted to decimal through binary. What is C9 in binary?
cards.why: Turn each hex digit into 4 bits, in order: C = 12 = 1100 and 9 = 1001, so C9 = 1100 1001 = 128 + 64 + 8 + 1 = 201.
cards.hook: One hex digit becomes one group of 4 bits, in the same order.

cards.q: A farmer must ferry a wolf, a goat and a cabbage from the east (E) to the west (W) bank. A state is written (farmer, wolf, goat, cabbage) and starts as (E, E, E, E). What is the desired final state?
cards.right: (W, W, W, W)
cards.why: The goal is for everyone to end up on the west bank, the farmer as well, so all four values are W: (W, W, W, W). (E, E, E, E) is the start.
cards.hook: Four slots, always: farmer first, then wolf, goat, cabbage.

cards.q: States are (farmer, wolf, goat, cabbage), each E or W bank. Without the farmer, the wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage. (W, E, E, W) is a loss state. Which of these is another loss state?
cards.right: (E, E, W, W)
cards.why: In (E, E, W, W) the farmer is on the east bank and the goat is alone with the cabbage on the west bank, so the goat eats the cabbage.
cards.hook: Loss = the goat away from the farmer, with the wolf or the cabbage.
keys: the goat is alone with the cabbage

cards.q: States are (farmer, wolf, goat, cabbage), each E or W bank. Without the farmer, the wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage. Why is (W, W, E, E) a loss state?
cards.right: The goat eats the cabbage on the east bank
wrong: The wolf eats the goat on the east bank
The wolf eats the goat on the west bank
It isn't: the farmer is with the wolf
cards.why: The farmer and the wolf are on the west bank, so the goat and the cabbage are left alone on the east bank and the goat eats the cabbage.
cards.hook: Read the slots in order: farmer, wolf, goat, cabbage.
keys: left alone on the east bank

cards.q: States are (farmer, wolf, goat, cabbage), each E or W bank. Without the farmer, the wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage. Which is a non-loss state, other than the start and the end?
cards.right: (W, E, W, E)
cards.why: In (W, E, W, E) the farmer is with the goat on the west bank, and the wolf and the cabbage are together on the east bank: a wolf doesn't eat cabbage.
cards.hook: Safe = the goat is with the farmer, or on its own.
keys: the farmer is with the goat

cards.q: Wolf, goat and cabbage puzzle: left without the farmer, the wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage. Which test tells you a state is safe?
cards.right: The goat is with the farmer or on its own
wrong: The wolf is with the farmer
The cabbage is with the farmer
The farmer is on the west bank
cards.why: Only the goat eats or is eaten. A state is safe if the goat is with the farmer, or alone on its bank, away from both the wolf and the cabbage.
cards.hook: Watch the goat: it is both the eater and the eaten.
keys: safe if the goat is with the farmer

cards.q: Chop Cup: move A swaps the cups at positions 1 and 2, B swaps positions 1 and 3, C swaps positions 2 and 3. The ball starts under the cup at position 1 and stays under that cup. Where is the ball after each move of ABCBCA?
cards.why: A moves it 1→2; B (1↔3) leaves 2; C moves it 2→3; B moves it 3→1; C (2↔3) leaves 1; A moves it 1→2. It ends at position 2, the middle cup.
cards.hook: Follow only the ball: a move changes it only if it swaps the ball's position.

cards.q: Chop Cup: move A swaps the cups at positions 1 and 2, B swaps positions 1 and 3, C swaps positions 2 and 3. Without knowing which cup the ball is under, which sequence of at least three moves always ends with the ball where it started?
cards.right: ABBA
cards.why: Each swap undoes itself, so ABBA is AB followed by its undo BA: every cup returns. ABA and ABCBA use an odd number of swaps, and ABAB cycles the three cups.
cards.hook: Undo in reverse: do some moves, then the same moves backwards.

cards.q: Chop Cup: each move (A, B or C) swaps two of the three cups. A sequence of at least three moves must put every cup back where it started. What is the shortest such sequence?
cards.right: 4 moves
cards.why: An odd number of swaps always leaves two cups swapped, so 3 or 5 moves can't work. Four can, e.g. ABBA, AABB or AAAA.
cards.hook: Swaps undo in pairs, so the length must be even.
keys: An odd number of swaps always leaves two cups swapped

cards.q: Quicksort the list 60, 30, 80, 40, 10, 50, 20, 70, 90 using the leftmost element as the pivot. What is the list after the first partition, if the sub-lists are not re-ordered?
cards.why: The pivot is 60. The smaller values keep their order on its left (30, 40, 10, 50, 20) and the bigger ones on its right (80, 70, 90): 60 is now in its final place.
cards.hook: Smaller left, pivot, bigger right: one partition, not a full sort.
keys: 60 is now in its final place

cards.q: Quicksort works by recursively partitioning a list about a pivot. What does one partition guarantee?
cards.right: The pivot is in its final sorted place
wrong: The list is split into equal halves
The smallest value is now first
cards.why: After a partition every smaller value is left of the pivot and every bigger one is right of it, so the pivot is where it belongs. The sub-lists are still unsorted.
cards.hook: Each partition locks one pivot into place.
keys: the pivot is where it belongs

cards.q: Why would 90 be a poor choice of pivot to partition the list 60, 30, 80, 40, 10, 50, 20, 70, 90 with quicksort?
cards.right: It's the largest: all 8 others go on one side
wrong: All 8 others would go in its right sub-list
A pivot must be the leftmost element
Quicksort can't use the largest value
cards.why: 90 is the largest value, so all eight others go to its left and none to its right. The list barely shrinks, so more partitions are needed and the sort takes longer.
cards.hook: A good pivot splits the list near the middle.

cards.q: Partition 60, 30, 80, 40, 10, 50, 20, 70, 90 about the pivot 90, as quicksort does. How many values end up in the left and right sub-lists?
cards.right: 8 left, 0 right
cards.why: Every other value is smaller than 90, so all 8 go to its left and the right sub-list is empty. The pivot itself is in neither sub-list.
cards.hook: The biggest pivot gives the most lopsided split.
keys: The pivot itself is in neither sub-list

cards.q: A flowchart inputs first_name, surname and date_of_birth (ddmmyyyy), sets first_name = first_name[0:2] and date_of_birth = date_of_birth[4:8], then outputs username = first_name + surname + date_of_birth. Name one input and one output.
cards.right: Input surname; output username
cards.why: first_name, surname and date_of_birth are read in (Steps 2 to 4) and username is shown at the end (Step 8). Name variables: values like Joe or JoSoap2003 get no marks.
cards.hook: Inputs come in before the processing; the output goes out after it.
keys: username is shown at the end

cards.q: In a flowchart such as the username generator (input first_name, surname, date_of_birth; output username), which shape shows an input or an output?
cards.right: Parallelogram
cards.why: Inputs and outputs (Steps 2 to 4 and Step 8) go in parallelograms. Rectangles are processes, diamonds are decisions and rounded ends are Start and Stop.
cards.hook: Slanted box = data in or out.

cards.q: Hubs A, B, C, D; road distances in km: A–B 20, A–C 15, A–D 15, B–C 25, B–D 30, C–D 35. A technician starts at A, visits every hub exactly once and returns to A. What is the shortest possible route?
cards.right: A→C→B→D→A: 85 km
cards.why: Only 3 round trips need checking: A B C D A = 20+25+35+15 = 95, A B D C A = 20+30+35+15 = 100, A C B D A = 15+25+30+15 = 85. Shortest: 85 km.
cards.hook: A round trip includes the last leg back to the start.

cards.q: Four hubs A, B, C, D are all joined by roads. A technician starts at A, visits each other hub once and returns to A. How many different round trips must be checked, if a route and its reverse count as one?
cards.why: From A the other three hubs can be visited in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 orders, but each route is the reverse of another, so 6 ÷ 2 = 3 different trips.
cards.hook: Fix the start, order the rest, halve for reverses: (n − 1)! ÷ 2.

cards.q: Figure 8 shows four digital hubs as lettered circles joined by straight lines labelled with distances in km. Which is a feature of abstraction in it?
cards.right: Scale and the landscape are left out
wrong: The route problem is split into sub-problems
The same pattern repeats for every hub
It lists the steps to find the shortest route
cards.why: Abstraction keeps only what the route problem needs: circles and letters for hubs, lines for roads, numbers for distances. Scale, rivers, hills and buildings are ignored.
cards.hook: Abstraction = keep what matters, drop the rest.
keys: keeps only what the route problem needs
Scale, rivers, hills and buildings are ignored

cards.q: Figure 8 models four digital hubs as circles A to D joined by lines. Which real-world detail does this abstraction keep?
cards.right: The distance between each pair of hubs
wrong: The real bends in each road
Each road's length drawn to scale
The rivers and hills along the way
cards.why: Each line is labelled with its distance in km, the one detail the route problem needs. The roads' shapes, the scale and the geography are left out.
cards.hook: Ask: does the problem need this detail? If not, abstract it away.
keys: labelled with its distance in km

cards.q: To plan her daily visits to the hubs in the shortest time possible, a technician uses heuristics. What is meant by a heuristic?
cards.right: A rule of thumb that finds a good answer fast
wrong: A method that always finds the optimal answer
Trying every route and picking the shortest
Splitting a problem into smaller parts
cards.why: A heuristic is a problem-solving shortcut that finds a good, approximate solution quickly when methods such as brute force would take too long. It may not be the best.
cards.hook: Heuristic: good enough, fast. Brute force: perfect, slow.
keys: brute force would take too long

cards.q: A technician must visit hundreds of hubs each day. Which of these is a heuristic she could use to plan her route?
cards.right: Always drive to the nearest unvisited hub
wrong: Work out the length of every possible route
Draw hubs as circles and roads as lines
cards.why: Always choosing the nearest hub not yet visited is a rule of thumb: quick and usually good. Checking every route is brute force, too slow for hundreds.
cards.hook: Nearest neighbour: the classic route heuristic.
keys: Always choosing the nearest hub not yet visited is a rule of thumb

cards.q: Which search algorithm suits the list Amir, Dean, Eoin, Helen, Natalia, Steve, Terry, with a correct justification?
cards.right: Binary: the names are already sorted
wrong: Binary: it works on any list
Linear: the names are already sorted
Binary: there are only seven names
cards.why: The names are in alphabetical order, which binary search needs, so it can halve the list each time. (Linear search, justified by the list being short, is also accepted.)
cards.hook: Binary search needs sorted data; linear search works on anything.

cards.q: List, in order, the names compared until Natalia is found by linear search in: Amir, Dean, Eoin, Helen, Natalia, Steve, Terry.
cards.right: Amir, Dean, Eoin, Helen, Natalia
wrong: Amir, Dean, Eoin, Helen, Natalia, Steve, Terry
cards.why: Linear search checks from the start, one name at a time: Amir, Dean, Eoin and Helen are not the key; Natalia, the fifth, is, and the search stops there.
cards.hook: Linear: start at the front, one by one, stop when found.

cards.q: List, in order, the names compared until Natalia is found by binary search, with mid = (lo + hi)//2, in: Amir, Dean, Eoin, Helen, Natalia, Steve, Terry.
cards.right: Helen, Steve, Natalia
cards.why: Positions 0–6: mid 3 is Helen, and Natalia comes later, so search 4–6. Mid 5 is Steve, and Natalia comes earlier, so search 4–4: Natalia, found.
cards.hook: Count the key too: the last compare is the one that finds it.

cards.q: Binary search for Natalia in Amir, Dean, Eoin, Helen, Natalia, Steve, Terry first compares her with Helen. Which names are still searched after that comparison?
cards.right: Natalia, Steve, Terry
cards.why: Natalia comes after Helen alphabetically, so she can only be in the right half. Helen is already checked: lo = mid + 1 leaves Natalia, Steve, Terry.
cards.hook: Throw away the half that can't hold the key, and the middle too.

cards.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search on a sorted list of size N?
cards.right: O(log N)
cards.why: Each comparison halves the part of the list still being searched, and N can only be halved about log₂ N times, so at most about log₂ N comparisons: O(log N).
cards.hook: Halving each step → about log N steps.
keys: halves the part of the list

cards.q: For a list of size N, what are linear search's worst-case and binary search's best-case time complexities?
cards.right: O(N) and O(1)
cards.why: Linear search's worst case checks all N items (the key is last or missing): O(N). Binary search's best case finds the key at the first middle it checks: O(1).
cards.hook: Best case: found on the first look. Worst case: the longest path.
keys: finds the key at the first middle it checks

cards.q: Binary search on the sorted names Amir, Dean, Eoin, Helen, Natalia, Steve, Terry. What is the most comparisons it can need to find one of the names?
cards.why: Each comparison removes the middle name and half of the rest: 7 names → 3 → 1. So any name is found within 3 comparisons, as log₂ 8 = 3.
cards.hook: Worst case for binary search ≈ log₂ N, rounded up.

cards.q: Linear and binary search both have a best case of O(1). What is meant by O(1) time complexity?
cards.right: Time stays the same whatever the input size
wrong: The time grows in step with the input size
It always takes exactly one second
The time grows slowly, like log N
cards.why: O(1), constant time, means the time needed stays constant regardless of the size of the input, N: doubling N doesn't change it.
cards.hook: O(1): the same few steps, however big the list.
keys: stays constant regardless of the size of the input

cards.q: Which of these takes O(1) time?
cards.right: A search that finds the key on its first check
wrong: Linear search when the key is last
Binary search in its worst case
Bubble sorting a list of N items
cards.why: If the key is at the first position checked, it takes one comparison however long the list is: constant time, O(1). It is the best case of both searches.
cards.hook: Constant time doesn't care how big N is.
keys: one comparison however long the list is

cards.q: In binary_search1, line 6 is `while (lo <= hi):`, line 7 is `mid = (lo + hi)//2`, lines 9–13 are an if/elif/else, line 14 is `return mid` and line 16 is `return len(L)`. On which lines does the iteration start and end?
cards.right: Starts on line 6, ends on line 14
wrong: Starts on line 7, ends on line 14
Starts on line 6, ends on line 16
Starts on line 3, ends on line 16
cards.why: The loop starts with the while statement on line 6, and its indented body runs to return mid on line 14. Line 16 only runs after the loop has finished.
cards.hook: A loop = its header line plus every indented line under it.

cards.q: binary_search1's loop sets `mid = (lo + hi)//2`, then `if L[mid] > v: hi = mid - 1`, `elif L[mid] < v: lo = mid + 1`, `else: return mid`. What happens on a pass where L[mid] < v?
cards.right: lo = mid + 1: search the right half
wrong: hi = mid - 1: search the left half
lo = mid: keep mid in the range
return mid: v has been found
cards.why: If the middle value is smaller than v, v can only be to its right, so lo moves to mid + 1. The range halves on each pass until v is found or lo passes hi.
cards.hook: Too small? Go right. Too big? Go left. Skip the middle both ways.
keys: The range halves on each pass

cards.q: binary_search1 loops `while (lo <= hi):`, moving lo or hi past the middle each pass, and returns mid when L[mid] == v. When does the loop stop if v is not in the list?
cards.right: When lo becomes greater than hi
wrong: When lo becomes equal to hi
After len(L) passes of the loop
When mid reaches the end of the list
cards.why: Each pass shrinks the range from lo to hi. If v isn't there, lo finally crosses over hi, the range is empty, the loop ends and the function returns len(L).
cards.hook: lo <= hi means there is still something left to search.

cards.q: Express the decimal number 121 as an 8-bit binary number.
cards.why: 121 = 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 1, so put 1s under 64, 32, 16, 8 and 1 and 0s under 128, 4 and 2: 0111 1001. Keep the leading 0 to make 8 bits.
cards.hook: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1: take the biggest that fits, every time.

cards.q: To write 121 in 8-bit binary, take off the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 whenever they fit. 128 doesn't fit; 64 and 32 do. What is left, and which place value is used next?
cards.right: 25 is left; 16 is used next
cards.hook: Biggest place value that fits, subtract, repeat.

cards.q: Squares 0–4 hold W W _ B B. A disc may slide into an adjacent empty square or jump over one disc into the empty square just beyond. Which sequence of moves (from → to) turns the row into B B _ W W?
cards.why: W_WBB, WBW_B, WBWB_, WB_BW, _BWBW, B_WBW, BBW_W, BB_WW. Each other option has two moves swapped, so a disc is sent onto a full square.
cards.hook: Keep the colours alternating so there is always a gap to move into.

cards.q: Squares 0–4 hold W W _ B B. A disc may slide into an adjacent empty square or jump over one disc into the empty square just beyond. What is the row after the moves 1→2, 3→1, 4→3, 2→4?
cards.right: W B _ B W
cards.why: 1→2 slides: W _ W B B. 3→1 jumps: W B W _ B. 4→3 slides: W B W B _. 2→4 jumps over square 3: W B _ B W.
cards.hook: Write out the whole row after every move.

cards.q: Row of shapes (S = square, T = triangle): S T T S T S T T S S. Each step: find the leftmost square and the rightmost triangle; if the square is to the right of the triangle, stop; otherwise swap them. What is the row after step 1?
cards.right: T T T S T S T S S S
wrong: T S T S T S T T S S
T T T S T S S T S S
T T T T T S S S S S
cards.why: The leftmost square is at position 1 and the rightmost triangle at position 8. Swapping them gives T T T S T S T S S S.
cards.hook: Leftmost square, rightmost triangle: swap from the two ends inward.

cards.q: Row of shapes (S = square, T = triangle): S T T S T S T T S S. Each step: find the leftmost square and the rightmost triangle; if the square is to the right of the triangle, stop; otherwise swap them. How many swaps are made before it stops?
cards.why: Swap 1: positions 1 and 8. Swap 2: positions 4 and 7, giving T T T T T S S S S S. Now the leftmost square (6) is right of the rightmost triangle (5): stop.
cards.hook: Each swap puts two shapes in place at once.

cards.q: An algorithm keeps swapping the leftmost square with the rightmost triangle until every triangle is left of every square. It provides 'a general solution'. What does that mean?
cards.right: It works for any number or order of shapes
wrong: It always uses the fewest possible swaps
It only solves this one row of 10 shapes
It is written in pseudocode, not code
cards.why: A general solution is a broad approach that always gives the correct output whatever the input: here, any arrangement and any number of squares and triangles.
cards.hook: General = works for every input, not just the example.
keys: always gives the correct output whatever the input

cards.q: A flowchart: Start → input a, b ('Enter two values') → t ← a → a ← b → b ← t → output a, b → Stop. What are the names of the two input variables?
cards.right: a and b
cards.why: The input box reads two values into a and b. t is not an input: it is given its value inside the algorithm (t ← a). 'Enter two values' is just the prompt.
cards.hook: An input variable gets its value from the user, not from ←.
keys: reads two values into a and b

cards.q: A flowchart reads two values, swaps them and displays them: t ← a, then a ← b, then b ← t. What is the purpose of the variable t?
cards.right: It holds a's old value so it isn't lost
wrong: It holds the total of a and b
It counts how many swaps are made
It stores the output to be displayed
cards.why: t is a temporary variable: it keeps a copy of a, because a ← b overwrites a. Then b ← t puts the old value of a into b.
cards.hook: To swap two full glasses you need a third, empty glass.

cards.q: To swap a and b, a student leaves out t and writes just a ← b, then b ← a. If a = 3 and b = 8 at the start, what are a and b at the end?
cards.why: a ← b makes a = 8, and the 3 is lost. b ← a then copies that 8 back into b, so both are 8. That is why t must keep a copy of a first.
cards.hook: Assignment overwrites: save the old value before you lose it.

cards.q: Flowcharts are commonly used in the design process to describe algorithms. Which is an advantage of using flowcharts?
cards.right: Visual, so the logic is easy to follow
wrong: They run faster than the finished code
The computer can execute them directly
They stay small even for complex algorithms
cards.why: A flowchart shows the flow and logic of an algorithm visually, so it is easier to understand than code, even for non-programmers, and it doesn't depend on any language.
cards.hook: Flowcharts are for people to read, not for computers to run.

cards.q: Flowcharts are commonly used in the design process to describe algorithms. Which is a disadvantage of using flowcharts?
cards.right: Unwieldy and slow to draw for big algorithms
wrong: They tie you to one programming language
They can't show decisions or loops
cards.why: For detailed, complex algorithms a flowchart gets huge and unwieldy and takes a lot of time to draw; a lack of standards can also cause confusion.
cards.hook: Great for small algorithms, a maze for big ones.
keys: takes a lot of time to draw

cards.q: State one advantage of sorting a data set.
cards.right: It lets you use binary search
wrong: Sorted data takes up less memory
Linear search only works on sorted data
Once sorted, it never needs sorting again
cards.why: Binary search requires a sorted data set and is far faster than linear search on big data. Sorted data is also easier to read and analyse (median, outliers).
cards.hook: Sort once, then search fast many times.
keys: Binary search requires a sorted data set

cards.q: State one disadvantage of sorting a data set.
cards.right: It takes time and uses CPU and memory
wrong: Sorted data can't be searched by linear search
Binary search is slower on sorted data
cards.why: Sorting algorithms take time and consume resources such as CPU and memory, with little benefit if the data is already nearly sorted, and new data must be kept in order.
cards.hook: Sorting has a cost: time and processing power.
keys: take time and consume resources such as CPU and memory

cards.q: values = [50, 70, 30, 60, 20] is bubble sorted by `for i in range(len(values)):` and inside it `for j in range(len(values)-1):`, swapping values[j] and values[j+1] when values[j] > values[j+1]. What is values after pass 1?
cards.why: Compare neighbours left to right: 50, 70 stay; then 70 swaps with 30, with 60 and with 20. The largest value, 70, bubbles to the end: 50, 30, 60, 20, 70.
cards.hook: After pass k, the k largest values are in place at the end.
keys: The largest value, 70, bubbles to the end

cards.q: values = [50, 70, 30, 60, 20] is bubble sorted by `for i in range(len(values)):` and inside it `for j in range(len(values)-1):`, swapping values[j] and values[j+1] when values[j] > values[j+1]. After pass 2 it is 30, 50, 20, 60, 70. What is it after pass 3?
cards.why: Pass 3: 30, 50 stay; 50 and 20 swap; 50, 60 and 60, 70 stay. That gives 30, 20, 50, 60, 70; pass 4 then swaps 30 and 20.
cards.hook: A small value moves only one place left in each pass.

cards.q: A bubble sort of [50, 70, 30, 60, 20] uses `for i in range(len(values)):` with no early stop. After pass 4 it is 20, 30, 50, 60, 70. Why is it the same after pass 5?
cards.right: It was sorted after pass 4; pass 5 still runs
wrong: Pass 5 swaps pairs back and forth
cards.why: range(len(values)) always makes 5 passes. The list is already sorted after pass 4, so pass 5 compares every pair but makes no swaps: still 20, 30, 50, 60, 70.
cards.hook: No early stop: every pass runs, even when nothing changes.

cards.q: A bubble sort uses `for i in range(len(values)):` and inside it `for j in range(len(values)-1):`, comparing values[j] with values[j+1]. How many comparisons does it make on a list of 5 values?
cards.why: 5 passes of 4 comparisons each: 5 × 4 = 20, which is n² − n. For large n that is about n², which is why bubble sort is O(n²).
cards.hook: n passes × (n − 1) compares ≈ n².

cards.q: A bubble sort uses `for i in range(len(values)):` and inside it `for j in range(len(values)-1):`, comparing values[j] with values[j+1]. It makes 20 comparisons on [50, 70, 30, 60, 20]. How many does it make on the sorted list [20, 30, 50, 60, 70]?
cards.why: It has no early stop, so it still makes 5 passes of 4 comparisons: 20. Its best case (sorted) and worst case (reversed) make the same number of comparisons.
cards.hook: O(n²) best and worst: this code never takes a shortcut.

cards.q: A bubble sort uses `for i in range(len(values)):` and inside it `for j in range(len(values)-1):`, comparing values[j] with values[j+1]. It makes 20 comparisons on 5 values. How many would it make on a list of 10 values?
cards.why: 10 passes of 9 comparisons: 10 × 9 = 90. Doubling the list multiplied the comparisons by about 4 (20 → 90): quadratic growth, O(n²).
cards.hook: Double n, and the work goes up about four times.

cards.q: A bubble sort uses `for i in range(len(values)):` and inside it `for j in range(len(values)-1):`, comparing values[j] with values[j+1]. Which change would reduce the number of comparisons needed?
cards.right: Stop when a pass makes no swaps
wrong: Run the outer loop one extra time
cards.why: Use a flag: set it to False at the start of each pass and True on a swap. A pass with no swaps means the list is sorted, so stop: a sorted list needs only one pass.
cards.hook: No swaps in a whole pass? Then it's sorted: stop.
keys: A pass with no swaps means the list is sorted

cards.q: Each bubble sort pass puts the largest remaining value at the end, so the inner loop is changed to `for j in range(len(values)-1-i):`. How many comparisons does it now make on 5 values?
cards.why: Pass i skips the i values already in place: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10 comparisons instead of 5 × 4 = 20. The sorted end is never compared again.
cards.hook: Don't re-check the end that's already sorted.

cards.q: A bubble sort of 5 values is improved with a swapped flag: if a pass makes no swaps, the loop stops. How many passes does it make on the already sorted list [20, 30, 50, 60, 70]?
cards.why: Pass 1 compares every pair, makes no swaps and leaves the flag False, so the loop stops after 1 pass. It still needs that pass to find out the list is sorted.
cards.hook: One clean pass proves the list is sorted.

cards.q: ASCII and Unicode are both character encoding systems. Compare them under the heading memory usage.
cards.right: ASCII 7 bits per character; Unicode 1–4 bytes
wrong: ASCII 1–4 bytes per character; Unicode 7 bits
ASCII 7 bytes per character; Unicode 1–4 bytes
Both use exactly 1 byte per character
cards.why: ASCII uses a fixed 7 bits (128 characters), so it is memory-efficient for English. Unicode uses 1 to 4 bytes per character: more memory, but over a million characters.
cards.hook: ASCII: small and English-only. Unicode: bigger and covers the world.

cards.q: ASCII and Unicode are both character encoding systems. Compare them under the heading compatibility.
cards.right: Unicode's first 128 codes are the ASCII codes
wrong: ASCII's 128 codes include all of Unicode
Unicode and ASCII share no codes
Only ASCII text works in every country
cards.why: Unicode is backward compatible with ASCII: its first 128 characters are the same. It also covers every language, so text works across countries.
cards.hook: Unicode starts where ASCII does: 'A' is 65 in both.

cards.q: Standard ASCII uses 7 bits for each character. How many different characters can it represent?
cards.why: 7 bits give 2⁷ = 128 different codes, numbered 0 to 127. Extended ASCII uses 8 bits for 2⁸ = 256; Unicode has room for over 1.1 million.
cards.hook: n bits give 2ⁿ codes, numbered 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.

cards.q: Ada, Grace, Joy and Kay each made a different project and got a different rank. The AI project came 1st. Grace came 3rd. Ada's web development project was not last. Kay beat the embedded-system maker. The data-analytics maker beat Joy. Where did Ada come?
cards.right: 2nd
cards.why: Ada did web development, so she wasn't 1st (that was the AI project) and she wasn't last. Grace came 3rd, so Ada came 2nd.
cards.hook: Each clue rules places out: the one left is the answer.

cards.q: Ada, Grace, Joy and Kay each made a different project and got a different rank. The AI project came 1st. Grace came 3rd. Ada's web development project was not last. Kay beat the embedded-system maker. The data-analytics maker beat Joy. Who came 1st?
cards.right: Kay
cards.why: Ada is 2nd and Grace 3rd, leaving Kay and Joy for 1st and 4th. Kay beat the embedded-system maker, so she can't be last: Kay came 1st, with the AI project.
cards.hook: Fix what a clue forces, then rule out the rest.

cards.q: Ada, Grace, Joy and Kay each made a different project and got a different rank. The AI project came 1st. Grace came 3rd. Ada's web development project was not last. Kay beat the embedded-system maker. The data-analytics maker beat Joy. Who came last, and with which project?
cards.right: Joy, embedded system
cards.why: Ada (web) is 2nd and Kay, who beat someone, is 1st, so Joy is last. The data-analytics maker beat Joy, so that is Grace, leaving Joy the embedded system.
cards.hook: Check the finished table against every clue once more.

cards.q: In web design the hex colour #0A33F0 gives red 0A, green 33 and blue F0, each from 00 to FF (0 to 255). What are its RGB decimal values?
cards.right: Red 10, green 51, blue 240
cards.why: Left digit counts 16s, right digit counts 1s: 0A = 0 × 16 + 10 = 10, 33 = 3 × 16 + 3 = 51, F0 = 15 × 16 + 0 = 240. So RGB(10, 51, 240).
cards.hook: Two hex digits: (left × 16) + right. A=10 … F=15.

cards.q: In the hex colour #0A33F0 the green component is 33 in hexadecimal. What is it in decimal?
cards.why: The left 3 counts sixteens and the right 3 counts ones: 3 × 16 + 3 = 48 + 3 = 51.
cards.hook: Hex 33 is not decimal 33: the left digit is worth 16.

cards.q: In the hex colour #0A33F0 the blue component is F0 in hexadecimal. What is it in decimal?
cards.why: F stands for 15 and counts sixteens; 0 counts ones: 15 × 16 + 0 = 240, near the maximum FF = 255, so the colour is mostly blue.
cards.hook: F = 15, the biggest hex digit; FF = 255.

cards.q: Finding a dice roll with yes/no questions: Algorithm 1 asks 1? 2? 3? 4? 5? in turn until a yes (a no to 5? means 6). Algorithm 2 asks ≥4?, then 3? or 6?, then 2? or 5?. Name each search algorithm.
cards.right: 1: linear search; 2: binary search
cards.why: Algorithm 1 checks one value at a time from the start: a linear search. Algorithm 2 splits the values left in half with each question: a binary search.
cards.hook: One at a time = linear. Halve each time = binary.

cards.q: Finding a dice roll with yes/no questions: Algorithm 1 asks 1? 2? 3? 4? 5? in turn until a yes (a no to 5? means 6). Algorithm 2 asks ≥4?, then 3? or 6?, then 2? or 5?. What is the most questions each algorithm can need?
cards.right: Algorithm 1: 5, Algorithm 2: 3
cards.why: Algorithm 1 needs 5 questions for a 5 or a 6 (tree depth 5). Algorithm 2 never needs more than 3, as each question halves what is left (depth 3): 2³ = 8 ≥ 6.
cards.hook: Tree depth = the worst-case number of questions.

cards.q: To find a dice roll, Algorithm 1 is a linear search (up to 5 yes/no questions) and Algorithm 2 a binary search (up to 3). Which is more efficient in general, and why?
cards.right: Binary: about log₂ n questions, not n
wrong: Linear: it always needs fewer questions
Binary: it never needs more than 2
Linear: it is O(log n), binary is O(n)
cards.why: Each binary question halves the options, so at worst it needs about log₂ n questions, O(log n), while a linear search can need about n, O(n). The gap grows with n.
cards.hook: Halving beats stepping: log n against n.

cards.q: This GCD code starts with a = 45, b = 18: `while a != b:` then `if a > b: a = a - b`, `elif b > a: b = b - a`, and finally `return a`. Which rows (a, b) of the trace table follow (45, 18)?
cards.why: 45 > 18, so a = 27; 27 > 18, so a = 9; now 18 > 9, so b = 9. a == b, so the loop stops: the GCD is 9.
cards.hook: New row each time a value changes; stop the moment a equals b.

cards.q: This GCD code starts with a = 45, b = 18: `while a != b:` then `if a > b: a = a - b`, `elif b > a: b = b - a`, and finally `return a`. What does gcd(45, 18) return?
cards.why: 45, 18 → 27, 18 → 9, 18 → 9, 9. The loop stops when a == b and returns a: 9, the largest number that divides both 45 and 18.
cards.hook: Subtract the smaller until they are equal: that is the GCD.

cards.q: Partition the list 29, 10, 14, 37, 13 about the pivot 13, as in one quicksort step, keeping the values in their original order. What are the two sub-lists?
cards.why: Only 10 is smaller than 13, so the left sub-list is [10]; 29, 14 and 37 are bigger, so the right one is [29, 14, 37]. The pivot 13 goes between them.
cards.hook: Leave the pivot out: it is already in its final place.

cards.q: Quicksort has partitioned 29, 10, 14, 37, 13 about the pivot 13 into [10] and [29, 14, 37]. What does it do next?
cards.right: Repeats the same process on each sub-list
wrong: Merges the sub-lists by comparing front items
Uses 13 again as the pivot for each side
cards.why: Quicksort is recursive: it partitions each sub-list the same way, with a new pivot, until every sub-list has one element (or none); then they are combined in order.
cards.hook: Divide and conquer: the same partition again on smaller and smaller lists.

cards.q: After quicksort partitions 29, 10, 14, 37, 13 about the pivot 13, the left sub-list is [10]. Why is it not partitioned again?
cards.right: A one-element list is already sorted
cards.why: A sub-list with only one element is already sorted, so the recursion stops there (the base case). [29, 14, 37] has 3 elements, so it is partitioned again.
cards.hook: One item: nothing to sort. That is where the recursion stops.

cards.q: Quicksort continues on the sub-list [29, 14, 37] with 37 as the new pivot, keeping the values in order. What are the two new sub-lists?
cards.right: Left [29, 14], right []
cards.why: 29 and 14 are both smaller than 37, so they form the left sub-list [29, 14] and the right one is empty. Then [29, 14] is split about 14, giving 10, 13, 14, 29, 37.
cards.hook: Smaller left, bigger right, the pivot in neither.

cards.q: Quicksort partitions a list around a chosen pivot. Which is a common strategy for selecting the pivot?
cards.right: The median of the first, middle and last
wrong: Always the largest value in the list
The mean of all the values
The value that occurs most often
cards.why: Common choices are the first, last or middle element, a random element, or the median of the first, middle and last elements. The largest value gives the worst split.
cards.hook: Pick a pivot likely to land near the middle.
keys: the median of the first, middle and last elements

cards.q: Figure 4 plots time against the number of values n for the curves O(n²) and O(n log n). What are quicksort's best and worst-case time complexities?
cards.right: Best O(n log n), worst O(n²)
wrong: Best O(n²), worst O(n log n)
Best O(log n), worst O(n log n)
cards.why: Best case O(n log n), the lower curve: even splits. Worst case O(n²), the steep curve: the pivot is always the smallest or largest value, so the splits are lopsided.
cards.hook: Even splits → n log n. Lopsided splits → n².
keys: Best case O(n log n), the lower curve
Worst case O(n²), the steep curve

cards.q: Why is quicksort's best-case time complexity O(n log n)?
cards.right: Even halves: about log n levels, n items each
wrong: Only log n items are ever compared
Each pivot removes just one item
cards.why: If every pivot splits its list into two equal halves, the recursion is about log n levels deep, and all n elements are processed at each level: n × log n.
cards.hook: Levels × work per level: log n × n.
keys: all n elements are processed at each level

cards.q: A quicksort always takes the first element of each sub-list as its pivot. Which input makes it hit its worst case, O(n²)?
cards.right: A list that is already sorted
wrong: A list whose first value is the median
A list with an even number of values
cards.why: On a sorted list the first element is always the smallest, so each split leaves n − 1 elements on one side and 0 on the other: n levels of about n work, O(n²).
cards.hook: Sorted input + first-element pivot = quicksort's worst case.
keys: the first element is always the smallest

cards.q: Driving test model (age, transmission, outcome): 18 manual FAIL; 22 auto PASS; 20 auto PASS; 19 manual FAIL; 30 auto PASS; 25 manual FAIL; 23 auto PASS; 17 manual FAIL; 19 manual FAIL; 21 manual PASS. Which pattern does it show?
cards.right: Every automatic driver passed
wrong: Every driver aged 20 or over passed
cards.why: All 4 automatic drivers passed, while 5 of the 6 manual drivers failed; and all 4 under-20s failed. But the 21-year-old manual driver passed and the 25-year-old failed.
cards.hook: A pattern must fit the data: check for the exceptions.

cards.q: Driving test model: the 5 candidates who passed had instructors with 5, 8, 12, 10 and 15 years' experience; the 5 who failed had 8, 3, 2, 6 and 5 years. Which pattern does it show?
cards.right: More instructor experience, more passes
wrong: Every instructor with 8+ years got a pass
cards.why: Passes average (5+8+12+10+15) ÷ 5 = 10 years of instructor experience, fails (8+3+2+6+5) ÷ 5 = 4.8. One 8-year instructor's pupil failed: a trend, not a rule.
cards.hook: Compare the averages of the two groups.

cards.q: Modelling and simulation help solve complex real-world problems. Why is abstraction important when developing a model?
cards.right: It keeps the key details and drops the rest
wrong: It splits the system into smaller problems
It includes every detail for exact results
It finds trends that repeat in the data
cards.why: Abstraction focuses on the most essential elements of a system and ignores unnecessary details, so the model is simple enough to understand, analyse and simulate.
cards.hook: Abstraction filters: keep what matters, hide the rest.
keys: simple enough to understand, analyse and simulate

cards.q: A student models driving test outcomes from gender, age, transmission and instructor experience. Using abstraction, which detail is best left out?
cards.right: The colour of the candidate's car
wrong: Whether the car is manual or automatic
Whether the test was a pass or a fail
cards.why: Abstraction keeps only what affects the outcome: age, transmission and experience stay, and the result is the output. The car's colour is an unnecessary detail.
cards.hook: Ask of each detail: does it change the outcome?
keys: The car's colour is an unnecessary detail
